column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article dates Eannatum to around 2460 BC; the entry dates the stele around 2450 BCE. The text gives no year. The article calls it the earliest known war monument, the entry one of the earliest; not repeated.
The entry dates Yermak's expedition 1581-82, the article 1581; no year given in the text.
The article puts his election as commander on 12 November 1945 (entry: November 1945, at 29), consistent.
Thin article; two sections only.
Short article; little beyond administrative history.

The entry says he was killed in a shoot-out at a Derg meeting; the article (Fikre Selassie Wogderess's memoirs) says those arrested were locked in a garage and summarily shot, and that a separate shootout followed in the evening, in which Major Yohannes Tiku killed Daniel Asfaw. The manner of death is left out. The article spells the captain both Almayahu and Alemayehu Haile; Alemayehu used.

The article gives Cảnh Thịnh's age at accession as 9 in the lead and 10 in the body; age left out. It also mentions a massacre of Han Chinese settlers in 1782 separately from the Gia Định massacre of 1776; only the latter told.
The article says passenger trains still run twice a week; frequency left out as it may change.
The article places Tezozomoc's height of power in the early 14th century, while the entry has Tepanec dominance in the early 15th century and his death in 1426; no century given in the text.
The article says the triptych is attributed to Memling; the entry names him as painter; authorship not restated. Thin article; two sections.

The article gives her birth as 353/2 or 346/5 BC (preferring the later) and says she was twenty-one at Alexander's death; the entry has c. 352. Birth year and age left out. The article dates the refuge at Pydna to 315 BC, the entry her capture to 316 BCE; year left out.

The article says the reservoir dam was completed on 20 May 2006 and the project by the end of 2008; the entry says 'completed in the 2000s'. Left the completion date out of the text to avoid a second dating.

The article dates his governorship of Hispania Citerior 179-178 BC (praetor in 180) and his birth around 220 BC; the entry says governor 180-178 and born c. 217. Both points left out. The article dates the marriage around 181 BC in one place and 172 BC in the Family section; left undated.
The article dates his accession to 1269 or 1270 in the lead but speaks of 'ascension to the throne in 1268' in the body; left undated.
The article is short; text is near the minimum length. The article's phrase 'other French units in Turkey were not affected' is unclear and was left out.
The article is short (about 350 words); much of it is already in the entry. Written close to the minimum; skip if too thin.
The article says Gisela was 'possibly' Charles's legitimate daughter and may have been at most five; left out.
The entry's siege of Zbarazh and the 1651 resumption of war are not in the article; not repeated or contradicted.

The article says he died 'at the age of 34', which disagrees with the entry's (and the article's own) birth in 1312/13; age left out. The article names the Dughlat amir Bulaji; the entry spells him Puladchi. Name left out of the text. The entry dates the conversion c. 1354; the article gives no date.
The article says he reigned only three and a half months, which sits awkwardly with an accession in 1516 after Marj Dabiq; left out.

The article says only that he was 'possibly murdered' by his son Mäxmüd; the entry says killed by Mahmud. His death is left out of the text. The article's dates for his early reigns disagree with each other (fled to Volga Bulgaria in 1423 in the lead, driven out by Baraq in 1422 in the body; khan 1419-1423, 1426, 1428); left undated.
SKIPPED: The article has one sentence of history (the Una Fort, home of the Bedi descendants of Guru Nanak); the rest is census figures, climate and transport, which would only pad the entry.
The article calls the united realm the Kingdom of Burgundy; the entry calls it the Kingdom of Arles. Used 'united Kingdom of Burgundy' without the other name.
The article says the movement 'was disbanded and its leading figures were arrested in December 1935' while the entry says Päts banned it in March 1934; the disbanding is left undated.

The article dates the Minox to 1936 ('entered the world market in 1936 with the development of the Minox'); the entry says from 1938. Left undated. The article also says the firm was renamed VEF in 1932 but calls it PTVGD up to 1940; left out.
Short article; written to about 280 words. The Greek and Kharosthi forms are given in the article with diacritics (Ooēmo Kadphisēs, Vi-ma Ka-lpi-śa); simplified here; restore if the checker flags.
The Vögte of Weida, Gera and Plauen and the House of Reuss are not in the article (it names only the Vogtland region beside the principalities of Reuss); not repeated.

The entry says the wadi was a route to gold mines from predynastic times; the article dates quarrying to the predynastic period but the beginning of gold mining to the Old Kingdom. The start of gold mining is left out.

The article gives his death as 709 or 710; the entry's dates end in 709. No year of death is printed. The article leaves open where his first diocese lay (York or only part of Deira); the text does not name the see.
The article's history section is short; the Ao granary of the entry is not in it.

The article names two builders of the temple: Sundarshan Shah in 1839 and Maharaja Pratap Shah of Tehri Garhwal. Neither name nor the date is printed; both were rulers of Tehri. The article gives the source as the Champasar Glacier at 4,421 m and elsewhere as the Yamunotri Glacier at 6,387 m; no name or height of the source is printed. The article places the hot springs at Janki Chatti, 7 km away, and also close to the temple (Surya Kund near the temple); the text follows the second.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (course, tributaries, basin area, a planned dam) and adds little to the entry
SKIPPED: article is about Yongcheng, a county-level city in Henan, not Yongcheng (Yong), the Qin capital near Fengxiang in Shaanxi: a different subject
The article's lead calls the picnic group the Patriotic Alliance, while its section on names says the Patriotic Alliance was a different, earlier group; the name is left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; it also dates his accession to 1213 against the entry's 1214

The entry calls Russian protection the first step in Russia's absorption of the steppe; the article cites a 2019 study that neither side saw it as annexation. Given as the study's view. The article does not say Baraq Sultan was of the Middle Juz, nor mention Orenburg.
The article says he became Lord of the Mercians shortly after 879; the entry says from about 881. No starting year is printed.
The entry says the troops asphyxiated hundreds of the Ouled Riah; the article says the whole tribe was suffocated. No figure or extent given in the text.
Left out the present dispute over the jathedar (SGPC appointee of 2025 versus the 2015 Sarbat Khalsa's appointees): a present-day matter.
Article gives birth as c. 5 September 1872; the entry's 1872 agrees. Did not give the day.
Left out audience figures, bureau counts, rankings and awards lists (present-day figures). Launch date 1 November 1996 agrees with the entry's November 1996.
Article's odd claim that 'Abd al-Jabbar was his pupil left out. Macdermott named as the article spells him, without a first name.

Entry says founded in the early 8th century; the article says end of the 7th or early 8th, most scholars favouring Ibn al-Nu'man in 698 CE (al-Bakri also gives 114 AH, 732/733, for Ibn al-Habhab). Founding year left out. Also left out 'largely rebuilt' wording beyond the completion date.
The article has nothing on the oil of the Albertine Graben that the entry mentions. 'History' used for the geological history of the drainage system, as the list has no better place heading.

Entry says Coloman abolished the duchy in 1107; article says 1107 or 1108: year left out. Entry calls him briefly king of Croatia; article says duke of Croatia 1091-1095: written as 'held Croatia' without a title. Article gives birth as c. 1070 or 1075.
The article names the Ottaways without first names. The entry gives 59 executed prisoners; the article gives no number, so none used.
The article does not mention the Diet of the Greater Republic meeting at Amapala (the entry does); not repeated. Short article: text kept near the minimum.

SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance and adds little to the entry; it also contradicts itself (report published 1476, before his return in April 1477; entry says printed 1487, article's works list 1487 but text says 1486)
Left out current leadership and the 2026 congress. García's presidency told only by the figures the article gives, its harsher wording left out.
Article dates his coronation at Pella to 150/149 BC; the entry says 149. Year left out of the text.
The article says Kuyper wrote Our Programme in 1877; left out. 'Won in 1917' in the entry matches the article's constitutional change of 1917.
The article says nothing of his government of Brabant from 1404 or of Antwerp, so those are not told here.
The article says he took the name Yoshiaki both on leaving the temple and on coming of age in April 1568; the name change is not told.

The entry says Mitsusuke assassinated him; the article says the blow was struck by his son Akamatsu Noriyasu on Mitsusuke's orders. The text says only that he was killed at the Akamatsu residence. The article also says he became shogun on the day of Yoshimochi's death (1428) and was appointed in 1429; the start year is left to the entry. The article calls Yoshimochi both the fourth and the fifth shogun.
The entry says the attackers killed him; the article says both that he decided to take his own life and that he was overrun. The manner of his death is not told.
SKIPPED: The article's history is a short paragraph on the two temples the entry already describes; the rest is census figures and present-day institutions.
SKIPPED: The article's history is three sentences on the Portuguese and Dutch fort, which the entry already gives; the rest is climate, economy and present-day banks.
The article gives his death as 29 May 1977 in the lead and 28 May 1977 in the body; only the month is given.

The entry dates the burial to 1995; the article gives lahar flows from 1991 to 1995, consistent. The long 'Bacolor before Martial Law' section, built on cited secondary works and general national history, was not used.
Left out the Bagoas of Heliodorus's Aethiopica and of Mary Renault's novel: fictional characters, probably not this man.
The article has the Landeswehr taking Riga on 22 May and the Freikorps on 23 May 1919.
The entry speaks of whisky distilling in the Speyside glens; the article mentions it only in the 2023 flag design, so it is not repeated.

The article dates the Nuzi record of Barattarna's death 'possibly around 1420, as per short chronology', which does not fit the entry's c. 1500 BCE; the date is left out. The text is short because the article is.
Entry says 'founded the United National Congress' and 'led the sugar workers' union': consistent with the article.
Article is fairly short; third section kept brief to avoid repeating the entry's statement on Greece's Civil Code.
Article gives the date 30 July 1570; entry says summer of 1570, consistent. Entry's 1573 elimination of the clans is not in the article and was not repeated.
Entry says Islam III Giray took Khmelnytsky with him; article agrees (taken hostage).
Entry already says it kept Transylvania free of raids for years; not repeated at length.
Entry says 'traditionally dated around 872 but possibly later'; the text gives the chronology debate without contradicting it.
Article dates the battle 499/496/493/489 BC; entry says traditionally c. 496 BCE, consistent.
Article: location disputed (Pelagonia or Kastoria; Boril's Wood; possibly near Vevi), date July or September 1259. Entry says the Pelagonia plain; location debate left out so as not to contradict it.
Article contradicts itself on which side was outnumbered (Cyrus said outnumbered, then 'the outnumbered Croesus withdrew'); that phrase left out. Article dates the battle 547 BC; entry c. 547 BCE.
Entry says the Sabis is usually identified with the Sambre; article says Turquin showed in 1955 it was the Selle near Saulzoir, the Sambre name 'arguably erroneous'. Location left out of the text.
Article gives the date 15 December 533 and places Tricamarum 17 miles / 150 stades west of Carthage; consistent with the entry.
Entry says Stephen had 'a much smaller army'; article gives Ottomans up to 30,000 or 120,000 against about 40,000 Moldavians. Army totals left out to avoid contradicting the entry.
Article's figures for Catholic membership and the CSU's place in politics left out as present-day matters.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words, nearly all already in the entry's description
Entry says he reigned from 1889; article says he ascended in January 1890. Accession date left out. The March 1889 attack is told without saying who ruled then.

The article counts his journeys inconsistently (six trips to Rome; five overseas voyages; 679 as his fifth and final trip to Rome): the text gives no number. Ecgfrith's grant of 685 of land south of the Wear (the 'sundered land', Sunderland) left out for length.

Left out: the article's claims of 'the largest regional economy' and contributions to the British Industrial Revolution, and Dhaka's population 'exceeding a million', as contested or promotional; the shipbuilding estimates of Indrajit Ray. The Maratha death toll of 400,000 is given in the article without attribution.

The article dates the revolt 740-743 and its start at Tangier to early 740; the entry gives 739-743. The text gives no starting year. Left out: the alleged Andalusian expedition to Tangier, which the article says modern historians discount; the Maragatos story (marked 'it is alleged').

The entry says he was murdered in 1359. The article says that 'in circumstances that remain unclear' he and Tughluq Beg were murdered in August/September 1359, but also that Natanzi and Otemish Hajji say he died of illness, and the Venetian notary Benedetto Bianco only that he died. The text does not say how he died. The article says contemporaries suspected him of his father's murder but that he appeared to be on good terms with his father, and gives Tughluq Beg or the ulus beys as the killers; the entry says he 'is said to have murdered' him. The text leaves out who killed Jani Beg.
SKIPPED: the article has no history: census figures of 2011, the carpet industry already in the description, a modern institute and two living cricketers; too little for a longer text

SKIPPED: the article has under 250 words of substance, and it contradicts the entry and itself on when Bilär was capital (entry: 11th and 12th centuries; article: 12th and 13th centuries, and also from the 10th to the early 13th) and gives the ruins as nearly 8 square kilometres against the entry's several
The article dates the first grotto to 'around 420 CE'; the entry speaks of a dated inscription of 420 in Cave 169, which the article does not mention. Consistent.
SKIPPED: the article has well under 250 words of substance: a short lead, one line on the chief shrine and a list of districts

The article gives both 8 July 1853 (entering the bay at Edo) and 14 July 1853 (arriving at Uraga) for Perry's arrival; the text says only July 1853. The article's lead says the Sakoku policy began in 1639 'after suppressing a rebellion'; its later section dates the Shimabara Rebellion's suppression to 1637. Both kept as the section gives them.

The entry says the princely states of Gujarat and the Deccan were merged from 1948; the article gives no year for the mergers. Kher's term is given as 1946-1952 in the article, before the state existed; the text omits his years. The article says 'southern Madhya Pradesh' for Vidarbha; kept as Madhya Pradesh.

The article says he acted as count from 945, that Sunyer retired in 947, and that he died in 993 (falling ill there in 993); the entry gives 927-992 and count from 947. The text gives no year for his start or his death. Hugh Capet's letter promised aid if Borrell preferred 'to obey us rather than the Ishmaelites'; left out for length.

The entry calls Russwurm 'one of the first Black graduates of any American college'; the article says the third. Consistent; not repeated. Left out: admissions statistics, rankings, the 2025 student encampment and recent presidents.

The entry calls the round tower one of only two in mainland Scotland; the article says one of only two in Scotland (the other at Abernethy). Not repeated. Left out: Storm Babet's evacuation of 2023 and the 2025 fire at the Maison Dieu church (brief recent events of little weight).
The entry's Swedish attacks on the city of Bremen in 1654 and 1666 are not in the given excerpt; not mentioned.

The article heads the last barge's section '1727 bucentaur' but says it was commissioned in 1719, begun in 1722 and first used in 1729; the entry says launched 1729. The text gives no launch year beyond what the entry has. The article mentions another bucentaur of 1449 'little known'; left out.

The article notes the disputed view, in some medieval sources, that the land was uninhabited when granted to the Knights; left out. Hermann von Salza's attempt to place the order under the papacy left out, as the entry already covers it.

The entry's account of Hosokawa Tadaoki receiving most of the province after Sekigahara and building Kokura castle is not in the article, which says only that Kokura Domain was ruled by the Ogasawara clan; not contradicted. The article gives Izuhara Domain the characters of Chizuka Domain, an evident slip; left out.

The article's summary section contains opinionated wording ('superpower', 'incompetent leadership'); not used. The article describes the Seljuks in the lead both as ending with Rum's collapse in 1308 and with the Seljuk Empire collapsing in 1194; the text follows the section's account and gives no end year beyond the entry's.
SKIPPED: the article has under 250 words of substance and adds almost nothing to the existing description (it covers the same funding dispute, Mytilene, Arginusae and his reputation)
The entry gives the river as about 90 kilometres long; the article gives 100.2 km. The text gives no length. The entry's Quentovic and the County of Flanders are not in the article; not mentioned.
The article does not mention the Maya research programme that the entry describes; nothing on it added. Present budget, portfolio and president left out (as-of figures).
Entry dates Black Tom Butler's manor house to around 1565; the article says c. 1560. Neither date given in the text.
Entry dates construction 1194-1197; the article gives 1193-7 in its history section. Text says only that it was finished in 1197.
Short article; text kept near the minimum. The entry's mention of the self-governing commune and Venetian era is not in the article.
Article states 80% of the world's silver came from this mine in the 16th-18th centuries, and calls it the richest source in history; not repeated.
Entry dates the move into Bructeri lands to around 98; the article says around 100 AD. The move itself is not retold.
The stele of King Jinheung and the Gyo-dong and Songhyeon-dong tombs named in the entry are not in the article.

The entry calls the pillar inscription the earliest dated inscription in Nepal and dates it 464 CE; the article says 'one of the oldest pillar inscriptions' and gives only Manadeva's reign 464-505. Neither claim repeated. The 1702 rebuilding is not in the article.
The entry dates the grant to the 1220s; the article gives 1226 for the agreement. The grant is not retold.
Article gives six months in Mecca in one quotation and seven months in another; no length stated. Van Heutsz called Colonel in the article, General in the entry; rank omitted.

SKIPPED: article has about 300 words, most of it already in the entry (formation 1356, 1895-1896 division, capital Gongju); too little to add; it also places the province in the southwest where the entry says centre-west
The entry dates Jugurtha's massacre of Italian traders to 112 BCE; the article gives no year for the siege and speaks of Romans defending Adherbal. No year given in the text.

Entry dates the murder of the brothers to 524; the article says 'in 525' by one account. No year given. Article gives death on 7 September 560 'at the age of thirty-eight', which conflicts with its own birth year 522 and with the entry's c. 560; only the feast day given.

The article gives the population as 5,112 in its lead and 4,994 usual residents in its demographics section, both for 2022; the lead figure used. The entry's 1890 birth year for Collins is not in the article.

The article says the code was not formally repealed at abolition and that the French parliament voted to repeal it in May and October 2026; the entry says it remained in force until slavery was abolished. Neither the end date nor the 2026 repeal is given. The article also says the code served until 1789.

The entry dates the party 1939-1989 and says it collapsed in 1989; the article treats it as still existing and rearmed after 2021. I told the post-2021 rearmament as a dated later event and did not call the party extant. The entry says it went underground in March 1948; the article gives the first shots on 2 April 1948. I gave only the 2 April date, which does not contradict the entry's underground move.
The article says Conan allied with Odo of Blois 'to defeat Judicael Berengar', who is also named as his father; this looks like a slip in the article, so I left out whom the alliance was against.
The article spells the societies 'compaginie della calza'; I wrote 'compaginie della calza' - check against the article spelling if the checker flags it.

The article gives the size of the Bolivar document collection inconsistently (22 volumes overall; 20 small volumes between 1824 and 1828; first edition in 1826), so I gave no number or year for it. The article calls him the first official President of Venezuela; the entry says first holder of executive power as a member of the triumvirate. I kept to the triumvirate wording.
The entry dates his rule from about 560; the article gives no year for his accession, so none is given.
The entry says the Taihō Code of 701; the article says the council was consolidated in the Taihō Code of 702. I gave no year for the Taihō Code.

The entry dates him as Minister of the Interior from 1892; the article says he headed the Ministry of the North from 1892, renamed Interior in 1894. I told both steps without saying he was Interior minister in 1892.
Panaretos is said by the article both never to mention David and to describe Tamar as Alexios' aunt; I mentioned only the first point.

The entry dates the Second Illyrian War to 219 BCE; the article places the fall of Pharos and Demetrius' flight in 218 BC. I gave no year for his flight. The article calls him Greek, half-Greek or Illyrian; the entry says Greek. I said only that he came from the Greek colony.
The entry says he defeated the Ambraciots at Olpae and Idomene; the article mentions only Olpae and the Spartan army there, so Idomene is not mentioned.
The entry says Irish hermits lived on islands north of Britain until driven out by Norse raiders; the article does not say this, so it is not repeated or contradicted.
The entry dates universal service to 1874; the article gives no year for it, so none is given. The Circassian quotation is paraphrased from the article's quoted words.
The entry speaks of Dudenev's raid in 1293; the article does not name it, describing only Andrey's coalition of Mongols and princes.

The article dates the duchy from 1102 (the archbishop's first seizure) and its passing to Prussia to 1815; the entry gives 1180-1816 and 1816. I gave 1102 only for the seizure, 1180 for the grant, and no year for the passing to Prussia. Ferdinand is called Ferdinand of Bavaria in the article; shortened to his brother Ferdinand.

The entry calls him the first of the hegemons; the article says he is commonly listed among the Five Hegemons. I did not call him the first. The article dates the punitive expedition against Wey to 671 BC, before the 667 BC conference that made him hegemon; left out.
The article is short; two sections.
The entry says the founding was 'around 71 AD'; the article gives 71 AD. I did not repeat the founding date.

The entry calls his fatwas on the Yazidis Suleiman's killings; the article adds Selim's attack on Cyprus, used here as 'Selim II' — the article says only 'his successor Selim'. If the checker flags 'Selim II', write 'his successor Selim'.
The article attributes the edict's preparation to Mahmud II (d. 1839) in one section and to Abdülmecid I's reign elsewhere; the text does not say who began work on it.

The entry says Kashta's tomb lies here; the article says Ku.8 'possibly' or 'presumably' belongs to him, so his tomb is not named in the text. Article's Shebitqo/Shebitku and Tanwetamani/Tantamani spellings; entry's forms used.

Death: entry gives 1404; article says 'June 1404' in the lead and 'around 1404' in the Death section; no year given in the text. The article contradicts itself on birth order (Eleanor second or third child) and on Aimery's son (William I or II); left out. Carta de Logu date 1392 is the entry's; the article gives none.

The article dates the Los Milagros aqueduct to the early 1st century BC, before the colony's founding in 25 BC; date left out. The bishop who built the Xenodoquio is called 'Bishop Mason' in the article (presumably Masona); name left out.

Entry says he ruled alone from 490; the article says he was largely in control by about 483 but she kept substantial powers until 490. Worded so as not to contradict. The summary dates the surname change with the 494-497 resistance; the narrative gives spring 496 for the surname edict and summer 495 for the dress and language edicts.

The article says he was in exile until 1931 and also took part in a Cuban uprising in August 1931; the order is unclear, left out. The article puts 'the following year' (1937) for 11th Division command but also October 1936 for Seseña; no year given for taking the division.

The article tells the 1241 sea battle twice: the capture of a papal fleet at Giglio, and a defeat of the Genoese fleet 'at Meloria' with captured churchmen; Meloria left out as a likely slip (the Battle of Giglio is the one with the prelates).
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words of substance, much of it a family list; little beyond the description

The article spells the historian 'Afaf Lufti al-Sayyid-Marsot'; written 'Lutfi' here — if the checker flags it, use the article's spelling. The article says he first arrived in Egypt in 1877 and became controller in 1879; also that he was raised to the peerage as Lord Cromer in 1892 — the earldom 1901.
The article says the looting continued 'until August 10'; left out as the chronicle's dating is approximate.

Article: Wen Zhong 'escaped to Qi, living his remaining days there' — doubtful (traditionally Wen Zhong was forced to suicide); left out. Entry calls his merchant name Taozhu Gong (Shiji); article writes Tao Zhugong; name not repeated.
Death: entry says d. c. 1038; article says c. 1040. No year given in the text.
Place of death disputed (Kingston in some records, Petit-Goâve per Jacques Nicolas Léger); not given.
The article dates Coronea to 446 BC in its lead and 447 BC in its body; the entry says 447. No year given in the text. Article's Cimon/Tanagra truce disputed (Kagan) and left out.
The article places the Second Zionist Congress in Cologne in May 1898 in one sentence; left out.
The article gives both 2,500 and 2,400 pages, and says the final version was completed in 1569 while Sahagún worked on it until 1590; page count and completion year left out.

Kept to dated facts; no assessment of present governments. The article's media section is polemical and unattributed in parts; left out. The lead says Verschave renamed the term in 1998 and that Houphouët-Boigny used it in 1955, while the etymology section calls that attribution mistaken; the etymology section followed, without contradicting the entry.
Pesaro: the entry says he received it in 1512, the article says he was made lord of Pesaro in 1513; year left out. Article: Italian Wars of 1521 (1523–1525) — years left out.

The entry says resistance at Aintab wore down the French; the article says the French besieged and captured Aintab on 9 February 1921 (a victory that came too late to change policy). The text states the capture as the article gives it.
The entry credits Schickhardt with founding Freudenstadt; the article says Frederick ordered it and does not name Schickhardt. Kept to the order of 1599.

The article places a campaign by the emir Mamlan both in the first year of Gagik's reign and at the Battle of Tsumb in 998; only the 998 battle is told. The article gives no date for the completion of Ani Cathedral (the entry: 1001); not dated here.

The article dates his death 3 May 1697 in the lead and 4 April 1697 in the text; only the year is given. The entry calls the 1696 battle Jao Modo; the article calls it Terelj's Zuunmod; the text gives neither name.
The article does not mention the exchange of Narbonne for Nemours (entry: 1507).
The article gives his birth as 1551/54 in the lead and 1554 in the text. The pen name Gazayi in the entry is not in the article.
The entry dates the strike 3 to 12 May; the article says 4 to 12 May (called to begin on 3 May at one minute to midnight). No start day is given in the text.
The claim that Rodney pioneered breaking the line is disputed in the article; left out.
The article's lead says Grey governed South Australia from 1841, the text May 1841 to October 1845; consistent with the entry.
Birth date given as 6 June 1897 (23 May Julian) in the article; he gave 1898 at the academy. Not stated in the text beyond the place.
The article gives his death as c. 442–448 in the lead and reports scholars arguing for 442, 448 or c. 437; the entry has c. 448. No year of death given in the text.

The article says Emperor Otto II divided the march, but Otto I reigned until 973; the text does not name who divided it. The entry says his rule reached the Oder; the article names the Bober and the Neisse.
Short article: most of it is the Italian text and translation of one canzone. No dates of life are given.

The article dates the Bijapur conquest to December 1649 in the history and to 1638 in the fort section, and the British capture to 1761 and 1762; no year given for either. The founder of the Nayak line is dated 1490–1521, while the entry says the Nayaks ruled from the early sixteenth century; no date given.

SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance: lists of divisions, attractions and products; its history (Sogaya, the Gaya tombs, the dinosaur footprints) is already in the entry, the only other fact being the Battle of Danghangpo of 1592
Article's lead also calls him an advocate of Japanese colonialism and a Pan-Asianist.

Left out the article's mention of the islands as a possible US military objective in a '2026 Iran war' (speculative). The article says the Iranian seizure was 30 November 1971, as the entry does; the date is not repeated.

The article (on the regency) says Gresik was an international trade centre from the 11th century; the entry says from the fourteenth century. The 11th-century claim is left out; the text keeps to the 14th century, which the article also gives for its rise as a main port. The article gives no year for Malik Ibrahim's burial (the entry has 1419).
